extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (Plato/Republic), literature and aesthetics scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical critique of imitative poetry and painting: criteria for judging imitation, its epistemic status, moral effects on the soul, and its place in the well-ordered city. Examines distinctions among creator/maker/imitator and the proper standards for artistic and moral evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold ontology of production (god, maker, imitator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects and their representations come in three orders: the ideal/form (God/nature), the craftsman who makes particular instances, and the painter/poet who imitates appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this hierarchy to judge the ontological status of works: only the first (the form) is true existence; the maker produces particulars that partake of the form; the imitator produces mere semblances or appearances. Example: there is the ideal bed, the carpenter's bed, and the painter's bed (an image).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitators are thrice removed from truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitative artists (painters, tragic poets) produce works that are three removes from the truth and from the original 'king' (the source/true maker).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat imitative works as inferior epistemically; they cannot yield true knowledge because they copy only appearances. This metric argues against granting imitative poetry the same authority as knowledge-bearing activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitators lack genuine knowledge of what they represent
rubrics_metrics.description: The imitative artist does not know the realities he imitates (e.g., a poet can depict a cobbler without knowing cobbling). He relies on appearance rather than technical or practical understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate artistic claims about practical or moral matters skeptically: if the artist lacks firsthand knowledge or use-experience, his depictions are not evidence of expertise. Anti-pattern: assuming poetic representation equals factual or technical competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art appeals to the inferior parts of the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation addresses and nourishes the irrational, passionate, and appearance-driven parts of the soul rather than the rational, measuring principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing an artwork's moral or educational suitability, consider which part of the soul it stimulates. Works that primarily excite irrational passions (rage, uncontrolled grief, lust) count negatively for civic and moral education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry fosters harmful emotions and improper sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets encourage spectators to indulge in passions (e.g., weeping over another's troubles) that the wise man would restrain in his own misfortune; this transmission of 'evil' emotions harms the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge poetic passages that glorify or beautify excessive lamentation, rage, or other unreasoned passions as morally dangerous. Anti-pattern: praising in performance what one would condemn in personal conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popularity does not indicate knowledge or truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody, rhythm, and beautiful language can deceive the ignorant into attributing expertise to poets; popularity or praise for a poem does not mean the poet possesses true knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate rhetorical or aesthetic skill with substantive understanding. Evaluate claims by checking for demonstrable knowledge or practical consequence rather than by aesthetic charm alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence relative to use (user-maker-imitator distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three arts regarding any object: the user (knows how to use it and thus knows its 'goodness'), the maker (constructs it and attains correct belief), and the imitator (who neither uses nor truly makes). Excellence is judged relative to intended use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an artifact or representation, consult those who use the thing to determine what counts as 'good'. For artistic representation, privilege testimony or standards from practitioners/users over imitators' depictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical measure and calculation as standards of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Measurement, calculation, and the rational principle rescue the mind from sensory illusion; the part of the soul that trusts measure is the better part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer standards based on measurement, proportion, and reason when resolving apparent contradictions of perception. Treat appeals to pure appearance as suspect unless they can be reconciled with rational standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitative art weakens rational governance of the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Because imitative poetry strengthens the irrational elements, it impairs the soul's harmony and the rule of reason; thus it is unsuitable for a well-ordered city or soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude or restrict works that habitually stimulate the lower elements of character if the aim is civic or personal virtue. Use this as a policy criterion for censorship in the ideal state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets are unreliable as educators or legislators
rubrics_metrics.description: If poets had real knowledge of virtue and civic wisdom they would have been followed as teachers and legislators, but historical record does not show poets acting effectively in these roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of claims that literature alone can provide political or educational guidance. Evaluate proposals for moral education by checking whether their authors have demonstrable practical achievements in forming communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation is primarily 'play' and not knowledge-producing
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation is likened to play or sport; it does not yield true opinion or knowledge because it only reproduces appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat imitative works as entertainment or emotional stimulation rather than sources of reliable instruction. Use other disciplines (craft, science, mathematics) for knowledge claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess emotional depiction by its fit with a well-governed soul
rubrics_metrics.description: A good person will moderate sorrow and behave according to reason and law; art that promotes unmoderated lamentation is contrary to the ideal temperament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating portrayals of emotion, prefer those that model reasoned moderation and self-governance. Penalize depictions that celebrate uncontrolled passions as exemplary.
